entire renewable energy program which is being attacked by the Government. The renewable energy program has been recognized by the OECD and by many other countries and international agencies as being a model program for energy conservation and substitution.
If we look at the projected spending of government Departments we see that in 1984-85, $33.8 million has been committed to energy conservation. By fiscal year 1985-86, that budget will be cut to $18.7 million. If we look at the budget for renewable energy, we see that in 1984-85, $38.4 million was committed, however by 1986-87, that budget will be chopped to $6.1 million. If we look at the budget for new liquid fuels for 1984-85, we see that $35.9 million has been committed, but by fiscal year 1986-87 that budget will be chopped to $15 million. There are drastic cuts in the whole field of renewable energy.
Members who took part in the special task force on renewable energy have made glowing speeches about the whole question of hydrogen and energy storage research, but that program, which has a budget of $6.5 million, is being wiped out by the Government in its drive toward complete eradication of renewable energy research and development programs. Canertech was set up in western Canada to develop research and innovative design and to assist private entrepreneurs in getting involved in renewable energy research, and it is being wiped out. The budget for that program is some $30.6 million. It is a very important program for western Canada.
Those are some of the concerns which I have with the legislation. Not only are we wiping out the two programs of oil substitution and conservation, we are taking Canada backwards toward the 1950s, the 1960s and the 1970s in energy design. We are taking the emphasis away from renewable energy conservation and returning it back to a dependence on oil. With the North Shore natural gas pipeline, which I previously mentioned, the savings amount to approximately half a million barrels of oil a year. That is about one-third of the production of oil in Canada for one day. It is one small pipeline which happens to be located within my constituency. If we looked around the entire country, we would see that there are many, many oil substitution opportunities which could be made that would result in similar savings.
I know the Government is on the defensive about this legislation. It is obviously a very bad move. The Government knows that Canadians are opposed to it because Canadians not only want to save energy, they want to save money. When Canadians buy natural gas furnaces and convert 25 or 30-year old oil furnaces to natural gas, they do not only have new heating units in their homes, but, with these programs, they have better insulation in their walls and ceilings which effect a 30 per cent or 35 per cent savings in their heating bills.
These programs were forward looking and were designed to benefit the country and at the same time the consumer. The programs also stimulated a lot of investment by consumers. Even though the Government provided a $800 grant under
Oil Substitution Act
COSP, often individual home owners would have to put an additional $1,500 toward the purchase of a furnace. If that person was in a high tax bracket of 45 or 50 per cent, the Government would recover half of the grant, so the net cost to the country was not very high. However, the net benefit was very high in the saving of oil. That is why, when the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources published its figures a couple of months ago on oil supply and demand in Canada, it showed that on a net basis Canada will be oil energy self-sufficient through to the end of the century. Much of the fact that we are oil self-sufficient only three years after the National Energy Program was announced is due to the fact that we have had the best oil conservation and substitution program of any country in the western world. I certainly think the Government is making a very bad mistake and I hope it will withdraw this legislation.

Then they expect us to undo in six months all the damage they did in 16 years.lt cannot be done and the Canadian people know it.
What will this Bill do? The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) suggested this morning that this program must be wonderful because we voted for it. He does not know what happened four years ago. The Liberal Government brought in a stack of Bills, including the COSP and CHIP programs, so we could not debate them in principle. The Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) put up a terrific fight, and the then Speaker of the House, Madam Sauve, ruled that the Government acted improperly in bringing in so many Bills all in one. That is why we rang the bells
Oil Substitution Act
for two weeks, to protect the people's right to debate issues in this House. We did not do it for the oil companies, we did it for the people. The Speaker supported what we did, so the Government finally brought in the separate Bills and we had a chance to debate the COSP and CHIP programs.
The big item then was conservation and the best program the Liberals could think of were COSP and CHIP. Naturally we supported the Bill when we had a chance to debate it. But we also pointed out a number of follies in the Bill, and I want to deal with one or two of those today. I am not going to say that those two programs have not done some good. They have. They have helped conserve oil. They have enabled some people who otherwise would not have been able to insulate their home or change their heating system to do so. But it also enabled a lot of people, who had the money to do it themselves, to take advantage of the program. We had no better example of that than this morning when the Hon. Member from the NDP said he took advantage of it. He was not poor. He took advantage of it, and he is not the only one. Hundreds of people did.
Many people have said to me they would not have converted but for the Government offering the $800. I was in one home where the wife said she was afraid of natural gas, she did not like it. Her husband said, "Natural gas is going to save us money, lady." That is what he called her, "lady". "So", he said, "I am going to do it". He was the boss of that house and so he did it. But he had the money to do it on his own if he had wanted to. But no, $800 was coming into his pocket out of government coffers. Of those people who accepted that $800 when they did not really need to, I wonder how many realize they were placing a debt on the young people of this country who will have to pay it for years, and years and years. They contributed to that debt. The Liberals talk about one little program but they forget that the people have to pay.
Another Liberal said, Mr. Speaker, that, "you're cutting it out", as if the Liberals never cut out a program. I would like to remind the Liberal Members who are here that a few years ago, when they brought in an excellent program, the first home ownership program, where they gave $3,000 to young couples who wanted to get a home for the first time, suddenly one week they cancelled it. The Minister extended it for a few days, but hundreds of people who had started their foundations were left out in the cold. The Liberals cancelled the program without debate, without notice. This Government is at least giving a little time for people who want to use the COSP or CHIP programs. They have time to insulate their homes with the use of this grant because we are not suddenly cutting it off. They have until March 31 under COSP. Members who have spoken either do not know what happened in the past or are trying to fool the people a little more.
I grew up in a coal mining area, Mr. Speaker. My dad and brothers were coal miners and I probably would have been too if they had not made me stay at school. We used coal for years. My mother said many times that she did not want natural gas. She was afraid of it because it explodes too easily.

March 4, 1985
Oil Substitution Act
She liked the coal so we hauled it from the pit and hauled out the ashes year after year and no one complained. We did not want a substitution program.
As the years went by, mines closed, oil and gas became more competitive, and coal couldn't keep up. At one time there would have been a revolution in the Drumheller valley if it had been suggested that we convert to gas. However, I saw the day when hundreds of former coal miners voted for a change to gas. They had to adapt to changing conditions. Now that entire valley is served with gas. I know what it means to change and I know that at times changes have to be made. However, the decision should be made in the home as much as possible.
There are a lot of new things happening today, Mr. Speaker. I received a letter the other day suggesting that we are not using our wind power. I have never been to Lethbridge when there has not been a wind storm. Consider the power they could generate. What about tidal power? I do not know very much about that, but I think it has great potential. What about solar energy? They laughed a few years ago when a chap was building his home and said that he was going to heat his home with the sun. He said that in a country which has 50 below zero weather he could build a house and keep it warm with the sun by conserving the sunshine. That home has no other power and they live comfortably in it winter and summer. That is conservation.
There are many ways to conserve. We should not be wasting oil and gas just because we have a lot of it. I had great faith in the Dean of Engineering at the University of Alberta. At one time he appeared before the Cabinet in Alberta and said that this good clean fuel, natural gas, is too valuable to be used by industry. He said that we should insist on industry using coal, the dirty fuel, and keep the nice, clean natural gas for the homes of the people. I thought that made sense. If we were short of natural gas, that would be the thing to do. However, we are not short of natural gas, and I do not think we are short of oil. We have the greatest reservoir of oil in the world in the tar sands of Alberta.
I was on a committee years ago to try to separate the oil from the sand. On my first trip to Fort McMurray I took a handful of sand and sqeezed it and found that there was oil all over my hand. Oil was oozing down the coulees. I thought that was a tremendous thing. We had a conference at which one of the professors of the University of Alberta said that he could separate the oil from the sand with a hot and cold water method. A pilot project was established with some public money and with the expertise of university professors. They found that they could separate the oil from the sand. Then others came forward with more modern techniques.
I remember standing in a plant in Fort MacMurray and seeing thousands of ton of beautiful white sand that people would love to have on a beach. From the other spout came the beautiful black oil that was going to go all over Canada. There are millions of barrels of oil waiting there to be separated if only we had the policy. However, the Liberal Government was too busy importing oil, closing up the sources in the country,
discouraging exploration, and importing oil. In 1980, the price to import a barrel of oil was around $31. The price to produce it in Alberta was about $16.50. However, the Liberal Government decided it wanted to import oil. It moved the exploration up north and gave PIP grants. They let the people in Alberta and Saskatchewan go without jobs.
There are still all kinds of oil in the Province of Alberta. We need an incentive program to search for it rather than a discouragement program such as the Liberals introduced. They continued to pay $31 of Canadian money for a barrel of oil. The Liberals then decided on the petroleum tax to make up the difference between the price of Canadian oil and imported oil. I think it amounted to 85 cents a barrel at that time which the people had to pay. The people of this country have paid and paid for the faulty Liberal policies which have discouraged the production of oil in this country and encouraged the importation of oil. They now stand up and talk about a shortage of oil.
I admit that this program has done some good and that conservation will not stop, but a lot of the people who took advantage of this $800 or 50 per cent of the cost to convert could have done it themselves. A lot of people will do it on their own. And yet many people, whom I really felt sorry for, were left out of the program entirely. The people in the small shacks around the coal mines in Drumheller could not afford the $3,000 required to convert. In some of those places they still use coal. The $800 grant was not sufficient for them because the conversion would probably cost $1,600 or $2,000. Where would they get the additional money? They just do not have it. They are retired coal miners who spent their lives in the bosom of the earth bringing out coal. They did not have that kind of money and could not take advantage of the program. Thousands of renters could not take advantage of the program.
Conservation will not end, Mr. Speaker. In March of this year COSP will end and in April of 1986 CHIP will end, but conservation will continue. The debt load that is being placed on the backs of the people through this program will be removed and conservation will continue with the people's own money, which is a far fairer program.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of comments and a couple of questions. I will first say how much I enjoy listening to the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). I do not agree with a lot of what he says, most of it as a matter of fact, but I enjoy hearing him. I have a great deal of respect for him because he has been around a lot longer than I have.
It is very impressive to hear the Hon. Member-who has a great deal of credibility-talk about actually seeing and feeling the oil in the tar-sands for the first time. I agree that the Liberals have short memories because our Party and the Conservatives, when in opposition, told them that the National Energy Program was a transfer of the exploration plays from the western sedimentary basin in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia to the North, to the Arctic and offshore.
March 4, 1985

The reason for this transfer is outlined in a new book entlitled Energy Politics in Canada, by Bruce Doehrn. It was simply a power play because the federal Government had jurisdiction in the Canada Lands and not in Saskatchewan and Alberta. I totally agreed with the Hon. Member when he said that this was a basic objective of the National Energy Program. We said so then and western Canada has paid for that transfer.
I agree with the Hon. Member that the Government must honour the contracts for the $1.6 billion in PIP grants. There are some questionable contracts, such as that with East Coast Energy Corporation, which must be phased out.
The Government stated its intention to replace PIP grants with tax incentives such as the superdepletion allowance and other tax rip-offs which helped the oil companies. If these only amount to PIP grants that are called tax breaks, I challenge the Hon. Member to vote against those tax changes. I believe the Hon. Member understands what I am saying and we will see what happens with the new schemes.
The Hon. Member also said that the Liberals taxed the oil industry out of existence. In 1982, the profits of Imperial Oil were $289 million. The latest report for 1984 shows that their profits are $533 million. Texaco went from $215 million to $423 million. Gulf went from $201 million in 1982 to $308 million in 1984. Shell went from $133 million in 1982 to $158 million in 1984. Given those figures which come from the business sections in the Financial Post and the Globe and Mail, could the Hon. Member explain how these companies were taxed out of existence? I do not believe that assertion to be correct.
The Hon. Member also said that Canadians would convert on their own to other forms of energy such as solar, tide and wind. I suggest Canadians will convert to other forms of energy only if they are paying too much for oil or if they are given an incentive to convert. Since I am in favour of providing an incentive for conversion, I suggest that these programs are justified. It makes sense to provide $500 when the home owner contributes $1,500. That is fair and it seemed to work well in the past.
Finally, one of the Government's first steps in dismantling the National Energy Program has been to eliminate the conversion measures in the program, that is, the off oil program and the insultation program. In my opinion, these were the only beneficial aspects of the National Energy Program. Would the Hon. Member, who is a sensible Canadian, explain why the Conservatives would dismantle, as its first step the only effective part of the National Energy Program.

subtopic: OIL SUBSTITUTION AND CONSERVATION ACT CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the effect of Bill C-24 will be to cancel a program and remove a potential $800 in grants toward the poor people of this country. Second, as a result of the action by the Government since it came to power, the heating oil prices have risen in this country. Another factor is that this Government, for the first time that I can recall in Canadian history, has developed a policy since January of selling oil cheaper to a foreign country than it is sold here. Since February 1, an oil company in the province which the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) was talking about, can sell a barrel of oil at the Chicago gate for about $5 a barrel cheaper than that barrel is sold at the gate in Toronto.
The other fact pertaining to this Bill is that people need that conversion grant in order to convert to alternate energy uses.
I think what I will deal with in my remarks is something that has not been dealt with adequately today in this debate, and that is, the conversion of oil to wood.
If you examine the statistics, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will find that the majority of conversions in Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, the Yukon and in the northern parts of this country have been toward wood. When you look at these grants, COSP, CHIP, RRAP, the programs initiated by Liberal administrations, there is one thing that everybody should keep in mind. These programs put money directly into the hands of the home owner. You can talk about lots of government programs that operate indirectly for the benefit of individuals, but these were transfer payments as outlined in the Estimates, transfer payments, as outlined by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), into people's pockets. These were the only grants people could get if they were living in a rural area and were below the poverty line. If they wanted to do anything at all with their houses, these were the only identifiable grants that put money actually
into people's pockets, primarily into the pockets of the poor people in this country.
I am surprised to hear the Members in this Chamber talking about where this money went. We have heard speaker after speaker in the Conservative Party say that some of that money, most of it or almost all of it, went into the pockets of people who really did not need the money. That is a complete fallacy. There are people who, if they did not get the $800, could not have converted to an alternate energy source. For example, how could somebody on welfare in those areas that I named convert to wood without the $800? How could somebody living on a pension convert to wood if he or she did not get that particular grant under COSP?
There were advantages to that program beyond the actual placing of money in the hands of an individual. The benefits can be seen in the provinces that utilize the wood conversion mechanism in the forestry sector. I am referring specifically to people who got cutting permits from provincial jurisdictions to utilize this grant program to convert to wood. They would take the tops of trees left by the paper companies which were strewn around all over the place in the forests. They also took the hard woods in the forests in which the paper companies are not all that interested. We still have pulp and paper companies that utilize just the soft woods. It is criminal in some places to see a paper company take the wood that was not hard wood. In other words, they would leave the birch trees and the like to die over a period of time, and leave the fallen tops to rot or start forest fires. I would say that the greatest assistance to the forestry industry is to have more people utilizing wood as a fuel source than anything else.
We have paper companies today that utilize herbicides, aerial spraying of herbicides, to get rid of the hard woods they do not want. Surely there can be a policy to allow the people of Canada who want to utilize wood as a source of fuel to go on company lands and take it, since the paper companies themselves are not all that interested in it.
There have been other remarks made today in which Members said that the $800 was a giveaway. I think the point was made that when you convert to wood in the northern areas the $800 does not even come close to the total conversion cost. Poor people have to do with just the $800, and they did using their own intelligence, so to speak. They left the hot water heater still on the furnace. That was the only portion used in the home for oil purposes. Apart from that, people took the idea of the wood stove or the wood furnace and usually put it in the basement of the house. They had their own duct system that came up to the main floor of the dwelling. It was not permissible for insurance purposes to plug in the wood stove with the furnace duct system, and there was a restriction in the program that you were not allowed to do it. There had to be a separate duct system, if that is what you were using. Or if you wanted to put in a completely new system with a wood and oil furnace, then that would be permissible under the rules.
For the poor people living on pensions, on welfare, on works programs, or on unemployment insurance, the obvious advantages in the rural areas to that gentleman in the example was
March 4, 1985

that he was able to instal a wood furnace with the $800. If he had not had that money, he would not have done it. He was able to utilize what materials he had in place in his particular dwelling. People normally had a chain saw. You would not use a buck saw these days and an axe. People normally had a chain saw and a snow machine to bring out the wood, a ski-do, as the Hon. Member for Prince Edward Island mentioned. In certain parts of the country they still have horses. A horse has even greater utility than a snow machine. First, a horse is cheaper to buy, although it costs more to feed. In certain areas of the country a horse is used as a means of hauling wood from the woods. Therefore, a person would save on the cost of a snow machine and a pick-up. People had a chain saw and transportation out of the woods. That is all they needed. They used their own muscles to supply themselves with heat. For what, Mr. Speaker? I will tell you. It was to save $200 a month. That is what they did it for, because that is what it cost in January, February, and March. When you look at ordinary people, say a widow with one son at home getting about $350 a month and having to pay out $200 a month to heat her home with oil, you can see what a saving it is to that person and how necessary it is.
The Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) mentioned that the ski-do or the snow machine was utilized in bringing in that wood for utility purposes. It is interesting that people in some parts of Canada actually believe that a snow machine is only used for recreation. Not at all, Mr. Speaker. It is used in conjunction with supplying the heating source in a home. That is the most important use of the snow machine. If the companies that build these machines would only look at that and keep producing the 12 horsepower and the 15 horsepower models, the best ones for that purpose, they would sell more snow machines.
The other point I should like to make is that the Government is saying that it is cancelling this program because it wants to cut back and because most people have utilized it. It is saying that there is no real need for the program and that it will be cancelled on March 31. There will always be a need for this particular program as long as we have people in the country who are relatively poor or live in areas where there is an adequate supply of wood. Thus we see the importance of this particular program.
The Government has turned around and cancelled COSP. It will also cancel CHIP and it has reduced the budget of other vital programs for home repairs which financially assist people. In particular, I am referring to RRAP, which goes hand in hand with the other two programs. It has been reduced to such an extent that in certain areas of the country it will be unworkable. We cannot have from 400 to 600 people on a waiting list for a program in which the delivery agent knows that probably only 50 of them can be approved because of substantial cut-backs. The general philosophy used by the Government in the cancellation of the program is wrong.
Oil Substitution Act
As I mentioned at the beginning of my intervention today, it is not good enough to have a policy of selling oil and reducing the charge to foreign countries. Since January 1 the charge went down 48 per cent for exported oil, heavy and light crude. The reason for this was obvious. The eventual product from oil was going into the United States at such low costs that the competition was too great for some of the oil companies in Alberta and Saskatchewan about which the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) spoke. To reduce the charge by 48 per cent to a foreign nation, to another country, without making the same reduction for refineries in Canada, is not good enough. To be able to sell a barrel of oil at $33.50 to an oil refinery in Chicago in the month of February and demand a charge of $39.50 for that same barrel at a refinery in Toronto is just not good enough.
There has been much discussion about the past Government and what it did, according to certain Hon. Members, to the oil industry, as well as about the foreign importation of oil to the East Coast. Mention was also made of the additional charges placed upon domestically consumed crude oil in Canada. The general philosophy behind this was to try to have some semblance of unity in the price of a barrel of oil, no matter if one was in British Columbia or in Newfoundland. That was the philosophy behind it, and it is a good philosophy. If we look at the refineries utilizing imported oil in eastern Canada, we find that there was always a mix of imported and domestically produced crude oil from western Canada which came via pipeline into Montreal. Those are the facts. Also there has been a declining demand for home heating oil in this country for the past three years to six years. The only increase in demand, if one looked at the figures, was in diesel fuel. Many oil companies in the country have made changes in their processes and are involved in different extractions and the building of petrochemical industries. All we have to do is to look at the enormous petrochemical complex at Sanford as well as the one at Sarnia, Ontario. We see a change taking place in the oil industry as far as what it does with oil and what is the demand at the other end are concerned. If we examine the entire industry, we will see that refineries have closed down in eastern Canada. Four closed in the Province of Quebec and three others in Atlantic Canada because the demand was not there for their product. At the same time we have seen a great increase in the number of petrochemical industries, especially in the Provinces of Quebec and Ontario. We are into ever changing times.
Let us look at the oil reserves to which reference was made earlier in the House. It has been said that they are good enough for Canada for about 14 years. No matter at what figures we look, normally they indicate that they are good for 14 years. If we go back 15 years, we find that they have always fluctuated-in the past they have been good for 14, 20, 15 and 10 years; now they are good for 14 years. However, that is not the important point. We have to look at the total production in Canada and wonder whether we are actually utilizing too much. Should we be exporting oil outside the country if we are in a tight squeeze? Should we be exporting oil out of Canada

March 4, 1985
Oil Substitution Act
and charging refineries in Chicago less than we are charging refineries in Canada?
This month the federal Cabinet was supposed to make a decision, in fact it was to be last Thursday. It was to be a decision on what would be the export charge of oil going into the United States. I do not believe that decision has been made, but I understand that since the demand for Canadian oil is increasing in the United States-and it fluctuates considerably from month to month-the export charge will be increased by about $2. That would mean that, for the month of March, instead of there being a $5 or $6 difference between the oil being sold in Chicago and the oil being sold in Canada, there will be a $2 or a $3 difference. If it is the philosophy of the Conservative Government to sell oil cheaper in the United States than it is selling oil in Canada, I am afraid the Government is in very serious trouble. It will not wash with Canadians. There is no way Canadians will put up with it. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) can turn around and say that that had to be done for the first time in Canadian history because the only thing that could be changed was the export charge, that they could not change the charges on domestic oil because we needed the money. However, we also need the money on the export charge. It makes no difference what taxes are levied on the domestic; there is always a tax on what is exported out of the country. It just does not add up, for the sake of conservation, to be cutting back and encouraging Canadians to use oil. That will be the only result of the move to cut back on CHIP and to cancel COSP. It will encourage Canadians to use more oil. However, are they being encouraged to pay more for oil than United States refineries? If the Government feels that it must cut programs which benefit the ordinary and poor people of the country, the very least it could do is to maintain the section of that program that was most utilized by the poor people, and I am referring to the section relating to the conversion to wood. There are not many people who are making $100,000 per year who will put a wood stove in their house to keep their families warm.
I know my time has run out, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion, let me say that if this is to be the continued direction of the new Government, it will have to do something different in three or four years' time in order to maintain its credibility.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) thoroughly expressed the views of the people from rural areas of Newfoundland and of the people across the country who happen to live in rural areas. I would like to make an observation and then put a short question to the Hon. Member.
The Hon. Member spoke about the increase in oil and gasoline prices and about the selling of oil and gasoline out of the country at lower prices than in Canada. His constituency is
similar to my own. The only exception is the Town of Gander in which wages may be a little higher. However, the outports in his constituency are similar to those in mine.
In 1964, I built my own home and installed an oil furnace. At that time, I was paying 18.3 cents a gallon for home heating fuel, and I still have the bills. Today, I am paying over $2.18 a gallon. Like me, the Hon. Member has many constituents who can be described as single parents who draw old age security and GIS and live in their own homes. These people have annual incomes of no more than $7,000. My electrical bill is $70 per month and, like most others, I have no extra frills or gadgets in my house. My oil bill in the month of February will run to approximately $400. I do not know if people understand the significance of that. We as Members of Parliament can afford to pay that amount because we are the fortunate people of the country. There are a great many people who are making a gross income of $7,000 per year and cannot afford to pay over $2,000 per year on home heat. Therefore, they have to convert to wood.
The provincial Department of Forestry in Prince Edward Island, aided and abetted by the previous federal Government and the present federal Government, has what I believe to be an excellent reforestation program. In Atlantic Canada, we have a problem with the spruce budworm. A great deal of wood is going to waste. The Department of Forestry cuts down the unwanted wood and puts it up for tender so these poor people can buy it at a good price. By converting to wood, their home heating probably costs between $400 and $500 per year. That is a tremendous saving. However, the Bill is taking that opportunity away from the ordinary Canadians who are striving to survive. The Government is trying to force these people into senior citizens' homes, thus costing the federal and provincial Governments three times as much.
As I see it, the Government is penny wise and dollar foolish. I wonder if the Hon. Member would comment briefly on that.

subtopic: OIL SUBSTITUTION AND CONSERVATION ACT CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. The Hon. Member's point is well taken. There are many family units being run by widows or by the unemployed. These people get to the point where they cannot afford those exorbitant oil and gas prices that are mainly caused by differences in provincial taxes. It is a heck of a lot different to be living in the Province of Alberta than it is to be living in the Province of Newfoundland where we must pay a flat rate on the bottom line of 22 per cent provincial tax. Those people to whom I have referred will be placed in a position in which they will have to convert to wood somehow. This Bill will discriminate against those people because it will take away from them the opportunity that was given to their neighbours. That is simply unfair to the poor people of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in this debate on the Bill before us, a Bill that would
March 4, 1985

effectively kill the conservation and off-oil program. I see that there are only a few minutes remaining to me. I wish to continue at a future time.
Perhaps at this time I could put on the record what I discovered while researching this topic. I went through the Senate hearings on energy and natural resources of June 1984 and I glanced through the submission made by the City of Whitehorse. At the end of that submission there are some figures regarding the costs of Canada for reducing our dependency on foreign oil. For example, it is stated that so far, according to Statistics Canada and the National Energy Program update, the Canadian Government has spent to the end of 1983 some $8 billion on new energy, some $3.4 billion on existing energy programs, and some $3.3 billion on the Oil Impact Compensation Program, making a total of $14.7 billion. In addition, as of June 1984, some $2 billion was committed beyond 1983 for the Western Canada Development Fund and some $.5 billion for the Atlantic Canada Development Fund, making a total of $17.2 billion committed to and spent on the National Energy Program. All of this created a total product reduction of some 6.7 per cent of 425,000 barrels, or a reduction of some 28,475 barrels per day. In other words, the submission indicated that after having spent some $17.2 billion, we reduced our dependency on foreign oil by some 28,475 barrels per day. However, so far the COSP and CHIP programs have reduced our dependency on foreign oil by over 60,000 barrels per day at a cost of only some $1.3 billion.
I do not understand the economics of the Government. I never understood the economics of the Liberal Government. It was willing to spend over $17 billion on reducing our dependency on foreign oil to the tune of only 23,000 barrels per day. The CHIP and COSP programs reduced our dependency on foreign oil by some 60,000 barrels of oil a day and only cost a little over $1 billion. However, it is the conservation programs that the Government wants to scrap. It is insanity.
I will continue my remarks when the Bill will be considered in the future.

["Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in the debate this afternoon on this very significant motion put by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges). The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Act, 1982, should be amended in section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to include a human foetus or unborn human being.
Having said that, I want to make it quite clear at this stage that I agree very strongly with that principle. I believe life does start at conception. I believe what we need is something to enshrine that principle in the law of the land. What better law can there be than the Charter of Rights?
Because this is such a very important principle, it is disappointing to me to see, notwithstanding the fact that there are snow storms swirling around us, that there is really just a handful of people in the House this afternoon to take part in this important debate. It is a debate that has had the attention
of the country focused on its subject for a long period of time. Looking back to the election campaign, I think that along with the issue of unemployment and capital punishment this had to be one of the main and principal issues during that time. This was an issue without any grey area. It was a black or white issue as far as the people of my riding and, I suspect, people across the country were concerned. They saw the issue as a matter of right or wrong. They did not see the issue as a question of maybe or compromise. It was strictly a matter of principle.
I think it is clear that there is a great gulf and a great difference of opinion between people in this country. While I do not share the ultimate opinion of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) on the principle we are debating here today, I do share a good many of her views and the concerns she has raised, particularly with respect to the whole concept of further debate, further discussion, and the further refining of this issue. I believe that if we go on from here, we will be on a collision path. A great many people have strong views on this issue.
I think probably those views have best been demonstrated recently in my own City of Toronto in the Dr. Henry Morgen-taler case. The issue received a full court hearing and review, but at the same time it left a strange feeling and a strange concern in the minds of a vast number of people, particularly on the issue of jury selection. I think it surprised a lot of people that there could be an organization whose main purpose was geared to advising on jury selection to produce a jury, if at all possible, that shared the views of one side or the other to such an extent that perhaps it could tip the balance in the case. When people learned there was a professional body that gave advice on the selection of a jury, and that in selecting the jury anyone who had strong religious feelings or convictions was not acceptable as a jury member, people in the City of Toronto and across the country felt there was something wrong with a judicial system of that sort. That although Dr. Morgentaler was acquitted on the charges, there was grave concern that the kind of jury selection we had was not really and truly a trial by Dr. Henry Morgentaler's peers. It is that feeling that has put in sharp perspective the conflict between the different points of view that we are dealing with in this significant issue.
If we proceed with an amendment at this time, I do not think there is very much doubt in the minds of those who feel very strongly one way or the other, as I do, that we will have a great confrontation, a confrontation that would probably put the whole prohibition issue of a number of years ago to shame. It could turn that issue into something very insignificant in comparison with this and in comparison with the kind of confrontation we could walk into if we take precipitous action.
I think this motion is a good one in that it starts to define the issues. It encourages debate and it does that not only on the streets, on television screens and on the radio, but in the House of Commons, the place where the debate will ultimately have to take place.
I believe we will have to have a lot more public debate before it is an appropriate time to deal firmly and once and for
March 4, 1985", 'all with this issue. There are a number of problems. The Hon. Member for Capilano touched on some of them that are involved in this issue besides those raised by the mover of the motion, the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe. Some of those concerns and problems have not, as yet, been addressed properly, in my view. One concerned the whole question of whether we enshrined this as a constitutional question.
I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating that my time has drawn to a close. I would like to have a future opportunity to expand on my views on this subject. I hope this debate will inspire the Government to bring forward further legislation. This will give all of us an opportunity to expand on our views in the House of Commons.']

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE HUMAN FOETUS
THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE HUMAN FOETUS
speechtext:
that:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Act, 1982, should be amended in section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to include a human foetus or unborn human being.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there is no question that this country has split into two decidedly hostile factions since the Criminal Code was amended in 1969 to exclude from prosecution those abortions performed for certain specific reasons in hospitals which have therapeutic abortion committees.
Those who feel that easy access to abortion is necessary to protect women who are unwillingly pregnant, state that a woman should be able to terminate an unwanted pregnancy freely, and that abortion should be available to all women, regardless of age, marital status or income level. Those who disagree base their reasoning on a definition of human life which was given by members of a scientific conference in Washington, D.C., which is as follows:
The majority of our group could find no point in time between the union of sperm and egg and the birth of the infant at which point we could say that this was not a human life. The changes occurring between implantation, a six-week embryo, a six-month foetus, a one-week child or a mature adult are merely at stages of development and maturation.
It is difficult, if not impossible, for those us who accept this concept of life to find a common ground on which to meet those who choose abortion as a means of ending pregnancy. Because there can be no common meeting ground, emotions run high and a feeling of hysteria is always in the air.
We who oppose abortion do so because we believe in the right to life. We are depicted by those who are opposed as unconcerned with the reality of the 15-year old girl who is pregnant because she does not know any better, or the mother of five who can see no way to support another child, or the mother who is carrying a defective child. We are seen as forcing a theory of life on a world which is torn by suffering and personal torment.
"Individual liberty" and "freedom of choice" are catch phrases that are fast gaining control of our society. Peoples' feelings are for what they can see, not for what someone has told them exists. Their eyes and minds focus on the woman, not on the child she carries. The sympathy is for the suffering of those already born, not for the one who is waiting to be

March 4, 1985
Constitution Act, 1982
born. They care not for the right to life, but only for the lives that are apparent.
Some time ago I received information on the stand of the Canadian Association for Repeal of the Abortion Law. Added to the information were copies of letters which were sent to the Badgley Commission. Without going into detail or individual cases, I would like to quote part of one letter which illustrates exactly what I mean by society's misunderstanding of the stand which is taken by the right-to-life groups in the country. It reads:
You are doubtless receiving many communications from anti-abortion crusaders. No one is asking them to have abortions. No one is denying them their right to believe that a fertilized ovum is a human person from the moment of conception.
No one expects them to campaign for birth control clinics which are also against their beliefs. These are basic religious freedoms. But the essence of religious freedom is that it applies to oneself, and not that one should force one's views on those who do not share them.
I think it is statements such as this which confuse and dismay, more than any of the hysterical accusations which are levelled at the pro-life organizations. It seems to imply that to fight abortion is to put a woman into a state of perpetual pregnancy.
I am against abortion, but I do believe in birth control and the education of the public regarding the various means of preventing conception. The public has become confused by the fact that those who favour abortion, state that they believe every woman should have the right to decide whether or not to carry a child. To them, abortion is a matter of personal conscience, and no woman should be forced to carry her child or terminate her pregnancy.
Aside from the fact that women can and have been frightened or manoeuvered into having abortions, the destruction of the child is the main issue. As long as I believe that life begins at conception, I will do everything in my power to prevent the termination of that life. The Canadian Association for the Repeal of the Abortion Law states that Canada must be willing to join the 64 per cent of the world where legal abortion is readily available. Their reasoning for this is that it prevents illegal abortions, that it faces the reality of abortion as a major health issue, and that it preserves the physical, mental, social and economic well-being of the women concerned. If it does all those things, it is a hypothesis which has not yet been proved.
The ends envisioned can be met through other means. Proper education solves many problems, especially when that education gives complete understanding of birth control methods which are available and a thorough understanding of the value of human life.
Man must learn that the preservation and continued growth of the human race demands more than ensuring that the poor have the same rights as the rich. It also demands that the weak must be protected from the strong, and the unborn from the mature.
The attempt to guarantee that the poor have the same rights as the rich was the main reason for the appointment of the
Badgley Commission. As I am sure everyone in this House knows, the Commission was to discover if the procedure was and is operating equitably across Canada. The terms of the Commission's appointment did not allow it to discover if the underlying policy was a just one, nor if the legal requirements to obtain an abortion were being met. By its very basic terms of reference, the Badgley Commission was destroyed as a forum for discussion of the abortion situation before it ever began. Those members of the general public and the medical profession who see abortion as the destruction of life could offer nothing to a commission which accepts abortion as a fact of life.
Finally, after intensive and prolonged research, the Commission discovered that the abortion law was not operating equitably across the country. The Commission pointed out that abortion is mainly available in major urban centres, and that many women still travel to the United States to obtain abortions because their hospitals do not have therapeutic abortion committees, or, if they do, the backlog is such that the child would be born before the abortion could be performed.
In addition, the Commission reported that there are also some hospitals with abortion committees which will not perform abortions just because a woman is pregnant. So the Badgley Commission proved that abortion is not offered equally across the country and that the rich and those who live in cities can obtain abortions almost on demand, while those who live in rural areas or small towns have much more difficulty, unless they are rich.
But one would think, in discussing a law, that an attempt would be made to gain justice for all and that the unborn child would be granted the same say as those who can speak for themselves. The concept of equality before the law demands that all participants be included, not just those who yell the loudest.
One of the means used by the Commission to discover if abortions were being granted equally was a survey of the hospitals in terms of total numbers, eligibility by provincial regulation, to have abortion committees, as defined and the number of those eligible which did in fact have abortion committees. It was discovered that of the 559 general hospitals across Canada which met the requirements for therapeutic abortion committees, only 271 or 48.5 per cent had done so.
Over half of the hospitals involved did not choose to have abortion committees. Their reasons for this included professional ethics of the staff, religious denomination, avoidance of conflict, and lack of demand for abortion. One of the staff members of a hospital responded to the survey by saying, and I quote:
Under the present circumstances, there is no longer any medical indication to justify therapeutic abortion to protect the life or physical health of the mother.
Some doctors themselves are now admitting that there is no medical reason for abortion. Even the late Dr. Gattmacha, who was one of the strongest allies of the abortion movement, stated; and I quote:
March 4, 1985

Today in our modern society it is possible to take almost any woman safely through her pregnancy except if she has cancer or leukemia, in which case an abortion would not save her life, much less prolong it.
One of the most definite problems for those fighting abortion and the destruction of innocent life, is that while there is proof that life begins in the initial or very early stages of a pregnancy, people are willing to destroy that life, to make the social and economic status of the mother more important than the right to life of those who cannot speak for themselves. We are fast losing sight of the traditional western ethic which has always placed emphasis on the basic worth and equal value of every human life regardless of its stage or condition. Short-range utility is taking the place of a code of ethics which grants to everyone the right to live his own life to the best of his ability.
By destroying another life to ensure one's economic and social success, the human race is losing whatever dignity and honour it has worked to build for itself over the centuries. It is right and proper that the individual be protected, that he or she be granted their God-given life and the right to grow and learn at his or her own rate. Unfortunately, all individuals are not granted the same rights. The legalization of abortion would imply that the end justifies the means and that destruction is allowable if a certain quality of life is preserved for those who remain.
Self-interest is held, then, to be more important than the common good. Truth becomes lost as man learns to define himself in terms of what he thinks is useful and convenient. To place a utilitarian value on human life, to see each person only in terms of his economic worth, can and will lead to the destruction of human life and can and will lead to the murder of those already born who through mental or physical incapacity are not able to contribute to society what may be demanded of them by extremists.
These and any other attempts to negate life, to state that it has no value in itself must never be tolerated. Life is an automatic value and the handicapped child has the same right as any other person to develop his full potential as a human being. Abortion, infanticide and mercy killing have a tendency to follow one upon the other. To destroy life at any level is to accept that all life has only relative value. Can those who propose the complete legalization of abortion guarantee that it will end there? Can they guarantee that the legal murder of the unborn will not lead society in general to other forms of murder? I think not, Mr. Speaker.
Conflict of interest automatically arises when attempts are made to legitimate the value of life. The abortion law in Canada, as it now stands, opens the doors wide to those hospitals in Canada who want abortion on demand. Statistics show that the number of abortions have increased by leaps and bounds, creating a situation whereby those hospitals which choose a lax interpretation of the law are now experiencing difficulty in dealing with the backlog. Needed elective surgery is backed up and operating theatres are constantly tied up. The abortionists would like to force the other hospitals and doctors into accepting this backlog. That must be prevented at all
Constitution Act, 1982
costs. Never do I want to see individuals and institutions forced into the taking of life, forced into the murder of those who are classified as unwanted, unwanted by a society that cannot be bothered with the question, let alone try to find an answer. Unwanted does not describe the child, merely the reaction of society of which he or she is a part. It is a state of mind, not a state of being.
In most of the disagreements and arguments that have taken place between pro-lifers and pro-abortionists, the focal point has been the issue of contraception. Those who favour abortion state that pro-lifers want to put women into a state of continual pregnancy. I have said before, and I must stress now, that proper birth control methods must be made readily available to all, and sex education must be taught in such a way as to make all people understand those methods. Money can and should be spent on the education of all people, not just those attending high school or college. Once that is done, people will be able to make the choice concerning the birth of children. As it stands now, abortion is becoming a means of contraception. Many women are choosing not to make full use of contraceptives. It has become much easier to terminate an unwanted pregnancy than to take the time to use proper birth control methods.
Destruction of the unborn child has become the accepted means of ensuring that a sexual relationship is not based on artificial means. Even the Badgley Commission agreed that the number of abortions will continue to rise if some means is not found to ensure that women have contraceptive protection. Its statistics show that 25.2 per cent of the women questioned who had abortions, discontinued use of contraception some time before the pregnancy; 27.2 per cent had not used contraception at any time. Those are definitely not hopeful statistics for the future children of Canada.
For those who do not want children, contraception is proper and necessary. For once conception takes place there can be no more contraception. Once a life has begun, it has the right to reach its natural end. That life has the same right to protection under the law as has its mother or any other of society. The right-to-life movement must be willing to show the people of this country that it does care. We must show that we are aware of the problems of illegal abortions and of the pregnant woman who needs assistance and guidance before, during and after her pregnancy. The public must learn what really we are trying to do, not what the pro-abortionists say we are trying to do.
Governments and the medical profession must be willing to offer assistance and explain exactly what that assistance is to women who are pregnant. The men cannot be forgotten either. The development of women's rights does not demand the end of male responsibility. A sexual relationship demands responsibility on both sides in the understanding and use of contraceptives and in the care of any child who may result from that relationship.
The legalization of abortion must be averted and the type of abortion available now must be ended before there will be any change in the values of Canadian society. To ensure that the

March 4, 1985
Constitution Act, 1982
intrinsic value of human life supersedes the monetary values of this nation, we must be willing to fight to prove that there are no fast, easy solutions to social problems. The pregnant woman and society must learn that killing the unborn child is not going to solve problems. The social problems which lead to unwanted pregnancy must be attacked at their base, through education, assistance and compassion. To insist that abortion be legalized because illegal abortion and maternal death will result if it is not, is much the same as saying that homicide should be legalized because murder will take place whether it is illegal or not.
The legal murder of the unborn must be stopped. Once that is done, all levels of society can join together to attempt to solve the social problems which are its cause. The sure way to do this, Mr. Speaker, is through this House, and that is, by amending the Constitution Act, 1982 to recognize the undeniable fact that unborn human persons have the same rights as other human beings, which is the right to life, liberty, and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof. Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, for the sake of all unborn children who cannot speak for themselves, we will see this happen in the not too distant future by taking the necessary steps to amend the Constitution and prevent the wholesale murder of unborn babies, which now exceeds some 80,000 lives per year from one end of our country to the other.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to take part in this debate on what is obviously a very important and sensitive question, indeed, one of the most difficult questions which faces this Parliament.
In approaching the motion of the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) who has just spoken, I feel it is important that we look carefully at the substance of that motion. The Hon. Member has suggested that the Constitution Act be amended in Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to include a human foetus or unborn human being. That is the motion of the Hon. Member. In analysing that motion, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that it is only appropriate that we look at the substance of Section 7 of the Charter of Rights. That section, under the heading "Legal Rights", reads as follows:
Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
In his remarks, which I listened to with care, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe quoted from Section 7 of the Charter, but in doing so he omitted the final words of that section. I am sure that was just an oversight, but the fact is that the Hon. Member's motion would permit the deprivation of life, liberty and security of the person in circumstances which accord with the principles of fundamental justice. I suggest to the Hon. Member that if his objective is to end all abortions in Canada today-and while I respect the view of the Hon. Member I disagree fundamentally with it-then he will not achieve that objective through the motion which is
before the House today. Far better, surely, to come before the House with a motion which would repeal those sections of the Criminal Code which permit therapeutic abortion and, presumably, return to the days in which all abortions in this country were illegal.
Having said that, I think it is only appropriate that I note that the position taken by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe is fundamentally different from the position taken by members of his caucus in 1981, including the seconder of his motion, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). Perhaps a bit of history on this matter would be in order. In November of 1981, the official spokesperson for the Progressive Conservative Party, then in opposition, moved the following motion. The Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) moved:
That the proposed Constitution Act 1981 be amended by adding after Clause 31 of Part 1 the following new clause:
"32. Nothing in this Charter affects the authority of Parliament to legislate
in respect of abortion."
The argument, made with considerable persuasiveness by the Hon. Member for Rosedale in November of 1981, was that there should be no amendment made to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which would deny Parliament, as the ultimate representative of the people, the right to legislate on the very difficult question of abortion. However, the motion before the House today would do precisely what the Hon. Member for Rosedale said this Parliament should not be doing. Indeed, it would entrench in the Constitution and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms certain rights of a foetus or an unborn human being. That flatly contradicts the position taken by the Hon. Member's colleague, including the Hon. Member for Bow River and the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) in November of 1981. I want to remind the House what those Hon. Members said in 1981. The Hon. Member for Rosedale said:
In my view, all sides of the House and, indeed, Canadians across the country, want to ensure that Parliament has the right to legislate if any changes are deemed necessary with respect to the law on abortion. The difficulty for a great number of Canadians is that conflicting legal difficulties throw that matter into doubt. We want to make it clear that Parliament's freedom to legislate on this matter is unimpaired.
Surely the Hon. Member who put forward this motion today and his colleagues who support it must recognize that it would do precisely what the Hon. Member for Rosedale suggested should not be done. It would indeed entrench in the Charter a specific provision on the question of abortion. The Hon. Member for Rosedale went on to say:
It took 350 years to establish the parliamentary system where legislation governing our actions with respect to life and death would be determined not by those appointed by the state but, rather, by those elected by the people themselves.
Members of this House applauded those sentiments, presumably including Members now on the Government side. He went on to say:
None of us disagree on that: not the Liberals, not the New Democrats, not the Conservatives, not Pro-Life, not Pro-Choice, and not anyone in the middle. We all agree that Parliament must have the freedom to decide. The purpose of this amendment is simply to make sure and to make clear to all that that is, indeed, our intention.
March 4, 1985

As I say, Mr. Speaker, that amendment was supported by Members of this House on the other side, so it was with considerable surprise indeed that I read the motion of the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe, which represents a complete reversal of the very reasonable position taken by his distinguished colleague from Rosedale.
