speechtext:
There are some Members on that side who will be given an opportunity to speak and, presumably, indicate if they oppose this motion, as they apparently did in 1981. I will look forward to hearing from those Members.
Certainly it is interesting to note this reversal of position, at least on the part of the Hon. Member for Bow River, who now supports a motion which flies directly in the face of the motion he supported in 1981.
As to the substance of the question, there are Members of this House who, in good conscience, believe that the Criminal Code should make no provision whatsoever for therapeutic abortion. I want to make it very clear that my position and the position of the NDP is that the provisions of the Criminal Code which deal with the question of therapeutic abortion should be repealed and the abortion decision should be one made by the woman in consultation with her doctor, that is, in terms of the provisions of the Code itself. However, we recognize as well that this is not just a legal question by any stretch of the imagination. It is essential that there be a whole series of other measures undertaken by Governments, both federal and provincial, to support women who are too often faced with the very difficult decision as to whether or not to give up a child because of economic circumstances. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is fundamentally wrong that the level of support for single parents in our society today is so appallingly low that there are still women, particularly single parents, who feel they cannot afford to have a child. That must be a concern of all Members of this House.
As well, we must support, indeed encourage, the funding of programs which enhance an awareness of sex education and family planning. We must also support the availability of safe contraceptive devices. I was pleased to note that the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe also supported that particular suggestion. When we talk about contraception, it is, I think, important that we recognize that contraception should not be solely the responsibility of women. The Ministry of National Health and Welfare should be undertaking research to deal with the whole question of contraceptive devices for males as well as for females. It is also important that family life programs and sex education programs be made a part of the regular school curriculum at both primary and secondary levels, and that this item be placed on the agenda of conferences between the federal Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) and his provincial counterparts.
It is fundamental to this issue that if we were to return to the days in which abortions were illegal in this country, that would not put an end to abortions. Rather, it would mean abortion would continue to be carried out in conditions which
Constitution Act, 1982
are often unsafe and, indeed, hazardous to the woman involved. The evidence shows very graphically that a woman who is desperate enough to want an abortion will have that abortion. Whether it be at the hands of a backstreet butcher, a self-induced abortion in conditions which are unsafe and hazardous, or whether she be forced, if she can afford to, to leave the jurisdiction and go to another province or outside the country, a woman will take the necessary steps if she is desperate and if abortions are made illegal. This has actually happened in other jurisdictions. For example, in Romania during the 1960s that country decided that because of certain demographic issues it wanted to tighten up considerably on its abortion law. The statistics showed that the number of abortion-related deaths increased markedly. To return to the days in which abortion was entirely illegal in the country would be an ultimately regressive and harmful move.
I would urge, Mr. Speaker, that we look very seriously at significantly increasing the funding made available to the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada and other organizations which are attempting to promote awareness of safe contraception and attempting to educate young people, adolescents in particular, about the importance of sex education.
In that regard, I would like to quote from a speech that was given in 1980 by the President of the Canadian Medical Association. It was a very thoughtful speech by Dr. W.D.S. Thomas. In that speech he urged the Government to repeal the present abortion law so that this would be a decision between a woman and her doctor, a position which the Canadian Medical Association has espoused since 1971. He urged that the Government increase, rather than cut, its funding for family planning programs. He went on to say the following:
I know that the best sex education program in the world will not eliminate unwanted pregnancies, it will not eliminate the need for therapeutic abortion, but it will help.
We need an educational program that will not only transmit the necessary information to teenagers, but one that will alter the basic value structure of our society. If we talk about conception control in isolation, isolated from other basic issues and values of society, our advice will fall on deaf ears. We have to deal with feelings and emotions, we have to talk to them about relationships, about decision making, about short term and long term effects of decisions, we have to talk to them about respect, what it is, how you get it, and how you show it. We have to be honest and open with them about sexual exploitation, about peer pressure for sexual gratification and its effects on a person's behaviour. We have to help them to clarify and adhere to their own personal values, we have to teach them that they have the right to say no, not just to sexual advances but to other things as well. We have to teach them about the different ways of showing affection and the advantages and disadvantages involved.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, he said:
More importantly, we must do a better job of teaching them how to build personal relationships, to understand the mental and emotional needs of themselves and others. With these foundations in place, with the proper attitudes, if teenagers are sexually active they will use birth control because of self respect and a sense of responsibility.
Many of us recognize that indeed there are too many abortions in Canada today. However, rather than repealing the provisions of the Code which allow for safe therapeutic abortions, albeit flawed provisions that discriminate between women in rural areas and other areas, and making all abor-

March 4, 1985
Constitution Act, 1982
tions illegal, we should consider the steps which I have indicated as being more appropriate in order to reduce the number of abortions. We must study sex education, consider better awareness and availability of contraceptives, and consider economic support for women who desperately want to keep their children. In some cases, as a result of the pathetic levels of human resources payments for women who are single parents, those women occasionally make the decision to give up their child.
I would like to applaud the steps which have been taken by the Government of Manitoba. That Government has recently embarked upon a very important funding program which enhanced the availability of contraceptives. It also expanded obstetric and gynaecological services at a number of Winnipeg hospitals. The Government of Manitoba funded a program of education and counselling on family planning as well. All these steps are very important and I would encourage other provincial Governments to look at them seriously.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, it would be a fundamental mistake for Parliament to accept the motion which has been put forward by the Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) and to entrench these particular rights in the Constitution itself. Some representatives who appeared before the constitution committee, of which I had the honour to serve as a member, urged that we entrench the concept of reproductive rights in the Constitution itself. Both sides were heard from on that issue and in the end Parliament decided that neither of them would be entrenched.
The logic of the Hon. Member for Rosedale was very compelling in 1981. It was so compelling that Members on that side of the House voted in virtual unanimity for the proposal that was made. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that logic is just as compelling today as it was in November of 1981.
In conclusion, I would urge that this Parliament recognize that Canadians, through one of the bulwarks of our criminal justice system in the country, that is the system of the jury, have sent a very clear message to parliamentarians. That message has been sent now by four juries in Canada in the case of Dr. Henry Morgentaler. That message surely must be recognized by Members of the House. That message is that the fundamental decision on abortion must be left to the woman in consultation with her doctor.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE HUMAN FOETUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), in introducing this motion to entrench constitutionally the rights of the unborn, feels very strongly about this issue. I always have admiration for people who have strong feelings about issues. His comments contribute to the public discussion on this debate, as have the comments of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). From listening to the comments of both previous speakers it is evident that, despite our differing views on the motion before us, we all believe that there must be further public recognition and public involvement in the prevention of unwanted pregnancies. We must ensure that all people take more responsibility in this area. If we had a motion
which suggested the advisability of the Government considering further work with the provinces and other groups in our society to increase funding and accessibility of information on those topics, we might indeed have all-Party agreement on it. That is the fundamental problem that we face.
Being a mother of teenagers and working with young people, I know that they are faced with such a barrage from the media and other sources in our society about their sexual involvement that sexual identification is extremely difficult. There is very little available to them with regard to the things that the Hon. Member for Burnaby brought forward. I remember one other time in the past six months when I agreed with the Hon. Member for Burnaby, and I do again today. I would like to have the quotation which he made from that doctor, because that expresses my feelings about what the thrust of our efforts should be and the direction that we as responsible parliamentarians should take.
The motion before us today does not address that issue. It is asking for the entrenchment of the rights of the unborn in the Constitution. I personally disagree with the motion, and I also think that it is an inappropriate way to bring about change on this issue. Whether the matter is abortion or dealing with constitutional change, it is one of the most serious issues facing Canadians.
I would like to address the subject of the appropriateness of trying to bring about change, first, in a Private Members' motion and, second, through constitutional reform. As Hon. Members know, I have my own Private Members' motion coming up next week with respect to that issue.
I believe that we need more time than available in Private Members' hour to discuss a major issue such as entrenching the rights of the unborn in the Constitution. We are all aware of how sensitive this issue is as a result of the barrage of viewpoints we received about this issue in our constituencies. I do not believe that there is a clear consensus in any part of the country.
There was a case in the United States. We should note what was said by Mr. Justice Blackmum of the United States Supreme Court in Roe versus Wade. He said:
We forthwith acknowledge our awareness of the sensitive and emotional nature of the abortion controversy, of the vigorous opposing views, even among physicians, and of the deep and seemingly absolute convictions that the subject inspires. One's philosophy, one's experiences, one's exposure to the raw edges of human existence, one's religious training, one's attitudes towards life and family and their values, and the moral standards one establishes and seeks to observe, are all likely to influence and to color one's thinking and conclusions about abortion.
I think it is evident here today that this is not an issue that divides on Party lines. Rather, it is a reflection of many of our own personal experiences. Having been involved in the women's movement in this country in many ways, I suppose that my own views are coloured by the kinds of experiences I have seen and been involved in. Certainly, I respect Members who hold different views on this issue.
March 4, 1985

The Hon. Member proposes to extend the rights in Section 7 of the Charter to a human foetus or an unborn human being. Section 7 guarantees to everyone the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. The issue of whether or not the Charter protects the rights of the unborn is already before the courts in at least two cases. They are very well known and publicized cases.
In the Borowski case, opponents of the present abortion provisions of the Criminal Code have argued that Section 7 of the charter does protect the rights of the unborn after a very thorough analysis of whether or not a foetus is a legal person. The trial court ruled that the term "everyone" in Section 7 did not include the unborn. That decision, as we all know, has been appealed.
In another case, Dr. Morgentaler argued that the restrictions on abortion in the Criminal Code conflicted with the mother's right to life, liberty and security of the person as guaranteed in Section 7 and with other provisions of the Charter. The Supreme Court of Ontario rejected this argument and held that the abortion provisions of the Criminal Code did not conflict with the Charter.
I am sure that we will hear more about the rights of the unborn under the Charter. Personally, I do not think that the fundamental controversy surrounding our abortion laws should be solved in the courts. I believe the issue is far too important. The courts have already indicated their discomfort at being placed in this position. After reviewing the history of the abortion laws in Canada in the Borowski decision, and noting that the present law had not had the effect of placating individuals or groups with an interest in the issue, Mr. Justice Matheson concluded in the Borowski case:
-it is the prerogative of Parliament, and not the courts, to enact whatever legislation may be considered appropriate to extend to the unborn any or all legal rights possessed by living persons. Because there is no existing basis in law which justifies a conclusion that foetuses are legal persons, and therefore within the scope of the term 'everyone' utilized in the Charter, the claim of the plaintiff must be dismissed.
Clearly, the question of rights for the unborn and whether or not abortions should be permitted and under what circumstances is an issue that concerns and divides Canadians. It is a very unfortunate division and something which I believe worries many of us. We need only to have watched our television in the last few weeks to see marchers and supporters and adversaries and opponents of abortion marching in Toronto in front of the Morgentaler clinic to put forward their views of our present law. As well, the polls which have been taken indicate that Canadians are seriously divided in their views as to what the law should be. As we are all aware on almost a daily basis, it is an issue on which those who do hold definite views are very reluctant to accept any compromise. In my opinion now is not an appropriate time to make a change in the law as such until we are able to develop a greater understanding and consensus among the public.
These are some of the reasons why I believe that Private Members' hour is not a suitable place to consider the issue of whether or not protection for the unborn should be put into the
Constitution Act, 1982
Constitution. We must make sure that we provide a full examination of all the issues.
If the Hon. Member is serious about changing the law, we should go about it in a different and proper way. First, we must make sure that we know what we mean when we say that we want to provide protection for the unborn. Second, we must be aware of what it means to add "human foetus" or "unborn human being" to Section 7 of the Charter. We are still at a very early stage of the interpretation of the Charter, and the provisions of Section 7 are being considered by our higher courts. We must also carefully assess the advantages and disadvantages of keeping our laws with respect to abortion in the Criminal Code.
I believe we should also keep in mind that there is an established process for amending the Constitution. Part V of the Constitution Act, 1982, provides that amendments must not only be approved by the Senate and House of Commons, but by resolutions of two-thirds of the provinces having at least 50 per cent of the population. This is a process which calls for close consultation with the provinces on the nature of the change to the Constitution and the impact it would have. If changes were proposed for Section 7 of the Charter to ensure protection of the unborn, this could have important implications for the provinces, especially in the area of family law. I do not believe that issue has been addressed by the Hon. Member.
Most important with respect to this issue, we must provide Canadians with an opportunity to make their views known on what the law should be. I do not think we can do that properly until we have done some of the things I have talked about at the outset and the other two speakers have talked about. We must make those kinds of fundamental changes in assisting young Canadians to become more responsible, to have a greater understanding and to have access to information and services. We should put the emphasis on the prevention of unwanted pregnancies rather than on having to deal with the growing number of abortions, many of which are related to the socio-economic conditions of the women involved who have not had access to appropriate information. Perhaps they have been reluctant to have access to that information. I think birth control information should be more publicly accessible to young women rather than in under-the-table discussions with girlfriends. I feel strongly about that, having a young daughter of my own.
Our Government believes in consultation and co-operation, a Government which consults before it makes fundamental changes in our laws. We take pride in involving Canadians in decisions on social benefits, housing and equality issues. We are proud of that record and it is one that we want to continue to maintain.
If we were going to consider changes in our abortion laws and to consider the Hon. Member's suggestion of enshrining protection for the unborn in the Constitution, we would have to make sure that individuals and groups with views on this issue could come forward to make those views known. This is an area in which we need consensus. I honestly believe that

March 4, 1985
Constitution Act, 1982
any legal changes that we might propose will not work. Potentially we would be in an even worse mess than we are today.
The Badgley report, to which the Hon. Member referred earlier, indicates that the present system is not perfect. It indicates that abortions are not available equitably across the country. We know that the present law does not work perfectly for people of either point of view.
While debate in Private Member's hour may touch on some of the issues and give us a better idea of what is involved, that is not the place to solve one of the most complex social issues facing Canada today. We must be sure that if we move to change our laws with respect to abortion, to protecting the unborn, we have the support of as many Canadians as possible. Without this we may be causing more problems than we are solving. In this forum we lack the time and the collective capacity to assess the complex issues involved in this one hour. We also need to ensure that we know as much as possible about the impact of any constitutional amendment in this area.
I urge all Hon. Members in this House to consider that whatever point of view they have on this issue, this is not the motion that is most urgently before us. We should be working together to solve the basic issue and working toward the greater awareness of Canadian men and women to ensure that there are no more unwanted pregnancies and that we bring a true sense of responsibility to our own sexual activities. If that were the direction we were to take, Mr. Speaker, we could all be very proud and optimistic about the results.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak in the debate today. I know it is an issue that will come forward at other times and in other forums. Through the opportunity to debate this issue and discuss some of its implications, we can learn about our different views, an interesting aspect to Private Member's hour. Perhaps in the next four years we will be able to reach some new approaches, new understandings, and new recognition on this whole issue of women and the unborn.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE HUMAN FOETUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in the debate this afternoon on this very significant motion put by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges). The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Act, 1982, should be amended in section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to include a human foetus or unborn human being.
Having said that, I want to make it quite clear at this stage that I agree very strongly with that principle. I believe life does start at conception. I believe what we need is something to enshrine that principle in the law of the land. What better law can there be than the Charter of Rights?
Because this is such a very important principle, it is disappointing to me to see, notwithstanding the fact that there are snow storms swirling around us, that there is really just a handful of people in the House this afternoon to take part in this important debate. It is a debate that has had the attention
of the country focused on its subject for a long period of time. Looking back to the election campaign, I think that along with the issue of unemployment and capital punishment this had to be one of the main and principal issues during that time. This was an issue without any grey area. It was a black or white issue as far as the people of my riding and, I suspect, people across the country were concerned. They saw the issue as a matter of right or wrong. They did not see the issue as a question of maybe or compromise. It was strictly a matter of principle.
I think it is clear that there is a great gulf and a great difference of opinion between people in this country. While I do not share the ultimate opinion of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) on the principle we are debating here today, I do share a good many of her views and the concerns she has raised, particularly with respect to the whole concept of further debate, further discussion, and the further refining of this issue. I believe that if we go on from here, we will be on a collision path. A great many people have strong views on this issue.
I think probably those views have best been demonstrated recently in my own City of Toronto in the Dr. Henry Morgen-taler case. The issue received a full court hearing and review, but at the same time it left a strange feeling and a strange concern in the minds of a vast number of people, particularly on the issue of jury selection. I think it surprised a lot of people that there could be an organization whose main purpose was geared to advising on jury selection to produce a jury, if at all possible, that shared the views of one side or the other to such an extent that perhaps it could tip the balance in the case. When people learned there was a professional body that gave advice on the selection of a jury, and that in selecting the jury anyone who had strong religious feelings or convictions was not acceptable as a jury member, people in the City of Toronto and across the country felt there was something wrong with a judicial system of that sort. That although Dr. Morgentaler was acquitted on the charges, there was grave concern that the kind of jury selection we had was not really and truly a trial by Dr. Henry Morgentaler's peers. It is that feeling that has put in sharp perspective the conflict between the different points of view that we are dealing with in this significant issue.
If we proceed with an amendment at this time, I do not think there is very much doubt in the minds of those who feel very strongly one way or the other, as I do, that we will have a great confrontation, a confrontation that would probably put the whole prohibition issue of a number of years ago to shame. It could turn that issue into something very insignificant in comparison with this and in comparison with the kind of confrontation we could walk into if we take precipitous action.
I think this motion is a good one in that it starts to define the issues. It encourages debate and it does that not only on the streets, on television screens and on the radio, but in the House of Commons, the place where the debate will ultimately have to take place.
I believe we will have to have a lot more public debate before it is an appropriate time to deal firmly and once and for
March 4, 1985

all with this issue. There are a number of problems. The Hon. Member for Capilano touched on some of them that are involved in this issue besides those raised by the mover of the motion, the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe. Some of those concerns and problems have not, as yet, been addressed properly, in my view. One concerned the whole question of whether we enshrined this as a constitutional question.
I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating that my time has drawn to a close. I would like to have a future opportunity to expand on my views on this subject. I hope this debate will inspire the Government to bring forward further legislation. This will give all of us an opportunity to expand on our views in the House of Commons.

subtopic: AUDITOR GENERAL-RECOMMENDATION THAT AUDITS BE REPORTED ON COMPLETION DATES
AUDITOR GENERAL-RECOMMENDATION THAT AUDITS BE REPORTED ON COMPLETION DATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 11, I asked a question of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) concerning the issue of the Auditor General being empowered to report more frequently to the House of Commons on a completion date basis rather than on an annual basis. I should like to discuss this issue to a little greater extent.
The Minister indicated that he was open to making the change. He referred to having had a meeting with the Auditor General, but he did not refer to the many recommendations of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. I should like to give a little history.
In July 1980, the Public Accounts Committee recommended that the Auditor General use more often his power to make special reports so that the Committee would be able more often to examine current issues. When a legal opinion was sought about these powers, the opinion was that in fact Sections 7 and 8 of the Auditor General Act did not contemplate regular, interval or completion date reporting and limited the Auditor General to reporting annually to the House of Commons, except in cases of special importance or urgency.
The legal remedy proposed was the insertion of the words "at least" in Subsection 7(1) and various consequential amendments to Subsection 7(3) and Subsection 8(1). Those changes were discussed at the time, and the President of the Treasury Board was in agreement, as was the then House Leader of the Official Opposition and the New Democratic
Adjournment Debate
Party caucus. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis), who I assume is answering this evening, is familiar with this matter since he as former chairman of the Public Accounts Committee put forward many of the recommendations to which I am referring.
In June 1984, in its fifth report to Parliament, the Public Accounts Committee again recommended the reporting of comprehensive and other audits on a completion date basis. Then on March 31, 1984 the Auditor General referred to the issue in his report.
The present situation is that the Public Accounts Committee very often deals with matters which are rather old because the Auditor General reports to Parliament in December on issues which have been audited by his staff many months before. In the case of a comprehensive audit, it is practice to allow Departments an opportunity to comment and for their comments to be included in the Auditor General's report. The constant recommendations for reporting on a more frequent basis were with the idea that the Public Accounts Committee could have before it matters which were more current.
If I may quote the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, in his previous role as committee chairman, he once said:
By the time the Public Accounts Committee reviews the comprehensive audit or the audit notes our review may be nothing more than a confirmation of the Auditor General's Report, rather than a useful exercise by a Parliamentary committee to reinforce the concerns of the Auditor General and make a public and departmental impact.
That was nicely said.
If the present President of the Treasury Board is willing to introduce a Bill which makes this simple amendment, the advantages of completion-date reporting as against waiting 12 to 18 months to get all the issues together would include the following. The subject matter of each release would be current in that it would have been recently completed and finalized by the Auditor General and his staff. The Public Accounts Committee would be more likely to review the matter thoroughly and enthusiastically because it was current. It would be more likely that a review would increase the effectiveness of the Auditor General's Report. The Public Accounts Committee would be able to plan its work better and the workload of the Auditor General would be distributed on a more even basis throughout the year. For all those reasons, I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary can tell us tonight that we will soon see this amendment to the Auditor General Act.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-ECONOMIC STATEMENT-IMPACT ON PROPOSED MANUFACTURING TECHNOLOGY INSTITUTE. (B) BACKGROUND DOCUMENTATION
THE ECONOMY-ECONOMIC STATEMENT-IMPACT ON PROPOSED MANUFACTURING TECHNOLOGY INSTITUTE. (B) BACKGROUND DOCUMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I raised a question in the House last November 13 with regard to the closure of the Manufacturing Technology Institute in Manitoba. I want to make a few comments today and I hope that the Government will take them into consideration in its long-term plans.
When the Government Party was running for office it promised tens of thousands of jobs overnight. It promised to replace confrontation with consultation and co-operation. It also promised that it would have a place at the Cabinet table for the West. It promised to bring western Canada into Government.
When we examine the specific instance of the handling of the Manufacturing Technology Institute in Manitoba, and when we examine the performance of the Government now
that it is in office relative to its promises during the election campaign, the Government gets very low marks. I am not only concerned about how it is rated in terms of its performance, I am concerned about its performance because that performance affects people in Manitoba.
The Government cut the Manufacturing Technology Institute last November, along with the many other cuts which were made in public spending. The Government cut that institute in spite of the lack of consultation which it promised when it was running for office. In spite of the fact that they promised consultation and co-operation during the election campaign, the Government cut that institute without any consultation with the people or the Government of Manitoba. The Government only met with the people of Manitoba concerning the question of funding for the Manufacturing Technology Institue after the question was raised in the House and pressure was put on the Government to meet with the people of Manitoba. Even though the Government then met with the people of Manitoba, the consultations were largely meaningless because they had no real impact upon the direction of the Government with respect to the Manufacturing Technology Institute.
The Government cut the institute in spite of the fact that it would have meant assistance to the private sector. It would have meant more secure jobs in Manitoba. When the Conservative Party was running for office, it promised to use the private sector as a means of job creation. This was an ideal opportunity to marry activity in the private sector with activity in the public sector and produce employment for Manitobans. However, the Government chose to cut back on this activity for some strange, inexplicable reason. It makes me wonder whether the Government sees no role for the public sector in assisting the private sector to grow, develop and provide employment. I wonder if the Government has such ideological blinders that it sees no role whatsoever for the public sector in encouraging private sector growth.
The Manufacturing Technology Institute was established to help manufacturers deal with new technologies-robotics, computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacturing- and the changes which are ongoing throughout the economy in relation to the new technologies. In spite of the fact that adjusting to new technologies is crucial to employment in Canada, the Government cut that institute. It cut an institute which would have had a positive impact on productivity. Rather than simply blaming our lack of productivity on wages, here was an opportunity to do something on the capital side of the equation to ensure productivity and continued employment.
The Government cut the Manufacturing Technology Institute in spite of the fact that there are a couple of Ministers from Manitoba who sit at the Cabinet table. It was the promise of the Conservative Party when it was running for office that there would be effective representation for the West at the Cabinet table.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-ECONOMIC STATEMENT-IMPACT ON PROPOSED MANUFACTURING TECHNOLOGY INSTITUTE. (B) BACKGROUND DOCUMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated before in this House, the decision to end the ongoing funding of the institute was not an easy one for the federal Government. Nor were we pleased to take the course. However, as with many of the difficult decisions which were announced on November 8, the Government is confronting the unpleasant fact that we cannot afford to do everything we would like.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party has said that the deficit should be treated as a long-term problem and should not colour our actions today. This statement ignores the fact that our actions today will have a long-term impact on the
Adjournment Debate
national debt. For example, the ongoing operating costs associated with the institute in Manitoba would have been in excess of $20 million per year.
Last November 13 the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) referred to the negative impact of the decision on the institute. Today he has said the same thing. In response, I would point out again that it would be difficult for anyone to credibly ascribe a specific impact to the decision. I say this because those involved in this very institute were still struggling to define the type of research and kinds of equipment the institute should have, and they did not even know then what to do with it.
As the Hon. Member will know, the previous Government was criticized by the Wright task force, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Senate Committee on National Finance. This institute was often cited specifically as a concern by those who criticized the policies of the previous Government. It was in this context that the November 8 decision was taken. Immediately, an effort was launched to find a more productive use for the IMT building. As the Minister said in Winnipeg last November, the building offers considerable potential and the Government is determined to see it put to productive use, notwithstanding the financial restraint which is facing the country.
In this regard, the Minister invited the private sector and the provincial Government to participate in the staffing and operation of the facilities. The Government believes that the private sector is more likely to take an interest in research and use it if it has a financial interest in the activity. It is for this reason that we are optimistic about the initiative of the Minister in relation to the Winnipeg institute. The Minister has already received several substantive proposals on the use of the facility. In February last he went to Winnipeg to continue consultations with the provincial Government and other interested parties.
